children.text: The gate Economics waits on

The Economics pillar asks whether a reform is sustainable. Under fee-for-service that question is answered after the fact, by an accountant. Under total-cost-of-care risk it has to be answered continuously, by an operator, while there is still time to change the outcome. That shift is what makes Technology a gate rather than a support function.

A hospital operating under a global budget is being asked to manage a fixed revenue envelope against a population's total spending. To do that it must know which patients are attributed to it, what those patients are costing, where that cost is accumulating, and which of it is avoidable — in time to intervene. None of those four facts is available from a billing system. They are the output of a data infrastructure that has to exist before the financial model is switched on.

This is the sequencing argument stated in infrastructure terms. Policy makes the reform permissible. Technology makes it possible. An organization that takes on downside risk before the data layer is built has not accelerated its transformation; it has agreed to be measured on a number it cannot see.
Three layers, not one system

Every state transformation runs on three distinct data assets, whatever the local acronyms happen to be: a claims database that shows total cost of care across payers, a clinical exchange that shows a patient's record across organizations, and an analytics capability that turns both into something a hospital or a regulator can act on.

In Vermont those are VHCURES, the all-payer claims database managed by the Green Mountain Care Board with Onpoint Health Data as aggregation vendor; VITL, the nonprofit that Vermont statute (18 V.S.A. § 9352) designates as the exclusive operator of the Vermont Health Information Exchange; and the analytics layer that AHS and GMCB have been jointly procuring, now organized around the Unified Health Data Space.

The common mistake is to treat these as three procurements. They are one system built in layers, and each layer is worthless for management purposes without the one beneath it. Vermont's own UHDS architecture makes the dependency explicit: foundational services establish who a patient is, exchange services move and store the data, and end-user services are what a clinician or a state analyst actually touches. Buy the top layer first and you have a dashboard reporting on an identity resolution problem.
What each data type can and cannot prove
What it records —
Claims: that a service was delivered, billed, and paid, and by whom → Clinical: what was found — diagnoses, lab results, vitals, medications, care plans
Total-spend visibility —
Yes — it is the only source that prices care across every setting and payer → No — a clinical record cannot price the intervention it documents
Quality measurement —
Systematically underestimates it — a claim shows an HbA1c was drawn, never the result → Has the result, but only for the population that organization happens to see
Typical latency —
12 to 18 months from service to analyzable record in VHCURES → Near-real-time where the provider is connected; absent where they are not
Failure mode when used alone —
A financial lag — you learn what the population cost you a year after you could have changed it → No total-spend view — you can avoid a duplicate test but cannot identify low-value volume

children.text: The four limits of a claims database

VHCURES is a genuinely strong asset. It produced the GMCB analysis showing Vermont hospital outpatient prices running from 279% to 697% of Medicare, the 32.3% potentially avoidable ED visit rate in the AHS transformation reports, and the drug affordability modeling behind the state's IRA analysis. Those are consequential findings that most states cannot produce. The limits below are not an argument against the database. They are an argument against using it as a management instrument.

First, coverage. Roughly 40% of commercially insured Vermonters are in ERISA self-insured employer plans. Vermont cannot compel those plans to submit. That is not a state failure — in Gobeille v. Liberty Mutual the Supreme Court held 6 to 2 that ERISA preempts state laws requiring self-insured plans to report claims data to a state database. Every state APCD in the country operates under the same ceiling.

Second, latency. VHCURES is collected quarterly, and analysts allow about six months for late claims to arrive — serviceable for retrospective research and useless for intervening in a patient's care. The November 2025 AHS transformation report acknowledged that most available measures reflected 2023 or earlier data.

Third, content. VHCURES holds medical and pharmacy claims. It does not hold mental health and substance use records governed by 42 CFR Part 2, social service utilization, housing status, or any other social determinant.

Fourth, and most consequential for quality, a claim is a billing record, not a clinical one. It shows that an HbA1c test was performed. It does not carry the result. This is why the hybrid measures Act 68 depends on — CMS 167 for hypertension control, CMS 204 for diabetes control — cannot be produced from claims alone. Absent clinical linkage, AHS told the Legislature in January 2026, provider groups and payers "must resort to manual chart abstraction" — paying staff to read charts by hand.
Gobeille is a federal ceiling, not a local failure

Act 68 can compel Vermont hospitals. It cannot compel a self-insured employer plan headquartered in another state, because ERISA preemption is federal and a state statute cannot reach it. Any transformation design that assumes complete commercial claims coverage has assumed away a constraint the Supreme Court has already ruled on. The honest response is to flag every population-level analysis as partial, pursue voluntary submission, and build the clinical data path that does not depend on payer reporting at all.
Managing blind — the OneCare case

OneCare Vermont was founded in 2013 by the University of Vermont Medical Center and Dartmouth-Hitchcock, and became the accountable care organization through which Vermont ran the federal All-Payer ACO Model from 2017. It wound down at the close of 2025.

OneCare took on downside financial risk for an attributed population. What it never assembled was the integrated data capability that managing that risk requires: a claims feed timely enough to act on, joined to a clinical feed complete enough to know what was happening to the patient. OneCare's own staff told the Green Mountain Care Board that its analytics lagged the newer software the UVM Health Network was adopting — an ACO at risk for a population's total cost, running behind one of its own members on the tooling.

The State Auditor's performance audits document what that looked like in outcomes. Patients attributed to OneCare had roughly 36% higher emergency department utilization and roughly 18% fewer primary care visits than peer ACOs — the exact pattern you would predict from an organization that could not identify rising-risk patients early enough to route them to primary care. A 2019 audit found OneCare did not reliably monitor or accurately report on community programs it was funding. Administrative costs ran $70.35 million between 2018 and 2022.

The financial bottom line is genuinely contested and should not be reduced to a single number — published estimates range from $18.23 million in savings to a net cost of tens of millions depending on whether the pandemic year is included. What is not contested is the mechanism. And the payer side closed the same way: Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont, the state's largest insurer, declined to renew effective January 1, 2023, withdrawing roughly 93,000 enrollees — about a third of total enrollment — citing data-protection concerns over OneCare's analytics subcontracting and the absence of evidence of improved outcomes or cost.

children.text: Why each feed alone is insufficient
State the failure precisely, because the generic version — "we need better data" — produces generic procurement.

Claims data alone creates a financial lag. You can see total spend, but you see it after the performance year in which you could have changed it, and you see it stripped of the clinical detail that would tell you why. Under fee-for-service that lag is merely expensive. Under a global budget it is disqualifying, because a hospital inside a fixed revenue envelope has to eliminate low-value volume specifically, and cannot eliminate what it cannot identify.

Clinical data alone gives no total-spend visibility. An exchange solves the narrow problem — a clinician can see that the same test was run last week at another hospital and not repeat it. Duplicate-test avoidance is the smallest version of the value question. The larger question is which of everything delivered to this population improved outcomes and which consumed resources without changing anything, and answering it requires knowing what a service cost, what it was meant to accomplish, and what happened afterward. Those three facts live in three systems.
Integration is therefore not a refinement of either asset. It is the capability, and neither asset delivers a usable fraction of it on its own.
The UHDS and the decision to lead with the faster feed

Vermont's answer is the Unified Health Data Space — not a second health information exchange but an implementation of the health data utility model, in which the combined clinical, claims, social and public health asset is treated as public infrastructure rather than any one participant's property.

Two statutory changes made it possible. Act 68 of 2025, section 10, mandated integration of clinical, claims and social determinant data into a single record per person. The quieter and more important change came in Act 167, which repealed 18 V.S.A. section 9410(e) — the provision that had barred the use of direct patient identifiers for record matching. Until that repeal Vermont's own statute forbade the technique its integration mandate requires.

The operational decision worth studying is which claims feed the state built on. Vermont routes integration primarily through the Medicaid Data Warehouse and Analytics Solution, which went live in early January 2026, rather than through VHCURES. MDWAS links Medicaid members' clinical data from the exchange with Medicaid claims inside the State's own system; VHCURES runs on a reporting lag of a year or more. For research, the lag is tolerable; for management, a timely feed on one payer beats a lagging feed on all of them. That is the correct trade, and it comes with an obligation: Medicaid is roughly a quarter of Vermont's primary coverage, so multi-payer scaling through 2029-2030 is not an enhancement to the plan, it is the plan.
Two claims feeds, two different jobs
Refresh cadence —
VHCURES: reporting lag of a year or more → MDWAS: linked Medicaid claims and clinical data in the State's own system
Population —
All payers, but only 60% of commercial → Medicaid only, scaling to Medicare 2026-2028
Consent model —
No patient opt-out mechanism → Integrated opt-out, compliant with Act 53
Fit for purpose —
Retrospective analysis, rate review, price transparency → Care management, risk stratification, global budget monitoring
Beyond Vermont: Maryland made the exchange a utility by statute

Maryland runs hospital global budgets through the HSCRC and needed the same substrate. In 2022 the General Assembly passed House Bill 1127, requiring the state-designated exchange, CRISP, to operate as a health data utility effective October 1, 2022 — the first law of its kind in the United States. It obliges the Maryland Department of Health, nursing homes, electronic health networks and prescription drug dispensers to supply data to the exchange, and obliges the exchange to deliver data in real time for treatment, care coordination and public health. The instructive point is the direction of travel: Maryland did not fund the exchange harder. It changed what the exchange was legally required to be. That is a Policy-pillar action taken in service of the Technology pillar, and it is the pattern any state should examine before writing another check.
The Equity Imperative at the gate
The sixth question — is it just? — is not a separate workstream. It is a test the Technology pillar has to pass on its own terms, and at the data layer it fails silently.

Vermont's own architecture documentation flags that race and ethnicity data is incomplete in commercial claims. That single gap propagates upward through every layer above it. Stratified quality reporting inherits it. Risk models inherit it. Equity monitoring under Act 68 inherits it. A state can hold a documented 13-point gap between white and Hispanic Vermonters on a 91% overall access measure, commit to closing it, and still be unable to demonstrate progress, because the denominator it needs is missing from the database it is measuring with.

This is what it means to say equity is a cross-cutting test rather than a pillar. Nobody has to oppose equity for the measurement to fail. The gap closes only if demographic completeness is a design requirement of the data layer itself — specified in the analytics procurement, not added as a reporting request afterward.
The diagnostic question

For any data asset, the question is not "do we have one?" It is: can an operator act on this inside the decision window that matters? A claims database with an 18-month lag and an exchange that most community providers have not joined can both be technically operational and jointly useless for managing risk. Ask what decision the data is supposed to support, then ask whether it arrives before that decision is made. If it does not, the asset is a research tool and the organization is not ready for downside risk.
What follows for sequencing

Vermont's Rural Health Transformation portfolio makes the dependency concrete. The transfer center and bed-availability tool, statewide e-consult, closed-loop referral, remote patient monitoring and the vendor-neutral imaging archive are each, in isolation, a vendor point solution. What converts any of them into measurable transformation is the data layer beneath. A transfer center works only if bed capacity and provider availability can be tied to a correctly matched patient record across every facility in real time.

Strip the substrate out and a large capital award becomes a set of disconnected purchases that cannot be attributed to a patient, linked to cost, or reported to CMS as evidence the investment worked. Capital arriving ahead of the data capability meant to carry it does not buy transformation.
That is the gate. Technology does not outrank Economics in importance — it precedes it in order, because the financial model cannot be operated without the visibility the data layer provides.

Distinguish what a claims database can prove from what a clinical exchange can prove, and name the blind spot each leaves
Identify the four structural limitations of an all-payer claims database used as a management tool
Diagnose the managing-blind failure mode in an organization that assumed downside risk ahead of its data capability
summary: Technology is the gate Economics waits on: no organization can manage total-cost-of-care risk it cannot see. This lesson works through Vermont's three-layer data architecture, the documented limits of its all-payer claims database, and the managing-blind failure mode that took down OneCare Vermont.
